title: The hurricane forecast cone shows where the eye may go, not how big the storm is
body: On 9 October 2026, Hurricane Isaias, the Atlantic's first hurricane of the year, made landfall near Destin, Florida, after days in which the US National Hurricane Center's forecast cone showed where it was heading. Many people read the cone as the size of the storm, but it only shows where the storm's centre will probably go. The [Hurricane Center](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml) builds it from its own past mistakes: at each forecast time it draws a circle big enough to hold two-thirds of the last five years' track errors, 72 km one day ahead and 370 km five days ahead in 2026, and the cone joins the circles. So the centre lands outside its circle about one time in three, and the storm is far bigger than its eye: Isaias's tropical-storm-force winds reached up to 335 km from its centre. In a 2026 study of 398 people in Florida and Georgia, those shown a newer version of the cone felt better able to judge the storm's size, which the map doesn't show.

slides.question: Out of 10 past forecasts, how many had the storm's centre end up inside the cone's circle for one day ahead?
slides.explanation: About 7 in 10: the US National Hurricane Center sizes each circle to hold two-thirds of the past five years' errors, so about 1 in 3 lands outside.

slides.alt: Animation on a sea chart: Hurricane Isaias nears the coast and a white forecast cone grows along a yellow track. Coral dots mark past forecast misses; a circle holds two of every three. Circles grow with time and join into the cone. Isaias's winds spread far wider. Then a 2026 study of 398 people.
slides.music: “Magic Scout - Nothern Glade” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Choose how far ahead a hurricane forecast looks, then size the circle until it holds two-thirds of the simulated misses.
slides.takeaway: About 72 km one day ahead, 176 km at three days and 370 km at five: forecasts miss by more the further ahead they look. Even then, one miss in three falls outside.

slides.heading: Radius of the 2026 Atlantic forecast cone's circles
slides.note: Each holds two-thirds of the 2021–2025 track errors (US National Hurricane Center)

left.label: It shows
left.text: Where the storm's centre will probably be at each forecast time, with about a 2-in-3 chance of being inside each circle.

right.label: It doesn't show
right.text: How big the storm is, or where wind, rain and surge will hit. Hurricane Isaias's tropical-storm-force winds reached 335 km from its centre.

slides.heading: A 2026 study
slides.text: Researchers at Florida State University showed 398 people in Florida and Georgia either the usual cone or a newer one that also maps inland watches and warnings. The newer map helped them find areas under watches, but its viewers also felt better able to judge the storm's size, which neither map shows.

slides.question: What sets the width of a hurricane forecast cone?
options: The size of past forecast errors
slides.explanation: Each circle is drawn to hold two-thirds of the last five years' track errors. The further ahead the forecast, the bigger the errors, so the wider the cone.

source.label: US National Hurricane Center: Definition of the NHC Track Forecast Cone (2026 radii)
